known_gaps.detail: The committed pages are stale relative to their template: regenerating applies the copy-voice rewrite they never received, and a sort-order and numeric-type normalisation in international-municipalities.v1.json. Refreshing that baseline is a separate reviewable change from un-committing, and is deliberately not bundled here.

Brazil's extractor mislabels budget_side on 454,916 rows. 101 revenue codes — ReceitaTributaria, Impostos, Taxas, TransferenciasCorrentes among them — arrive marked `expenditure` across all 5,570 municipalities, and none ever arrives marked `revenue`. The RREO column heading is authoritative (revenue uses PREVISÃO / No Bimestre / Até o Bimestre; expenditure uses DOTAÇÃO / DESPESAS), so the warehouse loader corrects from it and flags each corrected row side_corrected_from_source_column. The uniform layer and the committed per-municipality files still carry the defect, so the live site shows it until the extractor is fixed upstream or the fan-out is regenerated from a corrected view. Detectable only because Brazil publishes column labels; the other countries carry none, though their revenue-to-expenditure balances are all plausible.

The fan-out is stale where the warehouse is corrected. For BR:1100015 only 69 of 239 fan-out detail rows survive as-is: the files predate the budget_side repair and carry a different stage vocabulary (`cash`, `execution`) than the loaded lifecycle (`enacted → revised → committed → actual → paid`). The headline reconciles exactly, so the published figures are not at risk, but the two are not interchangeable and the fan-out is the wrong one. Retiring it needs prepare-public-serving-snapshots.mjs to build profiles from the warehouse and the entity directory rather than from these files.

Profiles now build from the warehouse (scripts/build-profiles-from-warehouse.mjs), and the headline they lead with was checked against every entity the site publishes, not a sample. Twelve countries agree exactly: Costa Rica 168/168, Georgia 276/276, El Salvador 518/518, Korea 486/486, Bolivia 686/686, Chile 690/690, Guatemala 680/680, Colombia 2,204/2,204, Mexico 4,760/4,760, Peru 3,782/3,782, Italy 15,792/15,792, Spain 20,978/20,978. Brazil is 11,070 of 11,114.

The derived headline rules are only as good as the entities sampled, and an even spread hides a year a small minority uses: 44 of Brazil's 5,570 municipalities report 2024 rather than 2025, so a 40-entity sample contained none of them and no 2024 rule was derived at all. Sampling is now stratified by year. A related accounting flaw is fixed too — a year with no workable rule used to drop out of both the display and the coverage sum, so a country missing an entire year's rule still reported 100%.

Brazil's 2024 DCA is loaded and its profiles reproduce every published headline: 11,114 of 11,114 across all 5,570 municipalities, both years. The 11,864 second-hand rows that came through the RREO loader were replaced by 12,046 read from the raw annexes, and the column heading is now kept in source_budget_item_type_code with FUNDEB deductions marked is_consolidation_item. Headline queries exclude consolidation items, without which a gross revenue and the deduction taken from it sum back together — the defect that inflated BR:1302405 by 7,265,266.90.

Denmark is re-extracted, loaded and serving. REGK100 across all seven dranst with ART=UE,I closes the accounts: Copenhagen 2025 is 68,818,554 thousand kroner out against 68,818,541 in, where the previous extract missed by 33,072,000. That extract was also wrong beyond the missing side — its dranst 1 operating expenditure was 31,850.3m against a true 55,925.2m. The 209,152 superseded regk31 rows were replaced by 70,145 from regk100; the budk32 enacted-budget rows were left alone, because REGK100 is the final accounts and replaces only the actual stage.

24 of Denmark's 196 entity-years do not balance in the source itself, by between 0.2% and 4.5% of expenditure, and one municipality reports negative gross expenditure — corrections flowing through a published series. The other 172 close to within rounding. This is recorded rather than absorbed into a tolerance: a threshold wide enough to swallow 4.5% would also swallow a real loading defect.

Denmark's headline rule is authored rather than derived, and the serving gate now distinguishes the two. A derived rule reproduces every figure the site already publishes; an authored one has no such check, so it is allowed only where the site publishes no headline at all and switching cannot regress one. Denmark qualifies on that basis, and its justification is recorded in municipal_headline_rules.json: the Danish account plan balances by construction, so a headline keeping financing in reports every municipality as revenue exactly equal to expenditure. Excluding financing — dranst 4, 5, 6 and borrowing under function 8.55 — gives Copenhagen 67.58bn against 67.12bn, a 0.46bn surplus, and across 196 entity-years the ratio runs 0.952 to 1.075 with 148 in surplus.

Japan is loaded and every published headline reproduces: 3,482 of 3,482 across 1,741 municipalities. The survey's structure ties exactly — table 02 row 01 (令和6年度) carries 歳入総額 and 歳出総額; table 05 row 33 （歳入合計）equals the first for 3,063 of 3,063 municipalities and table 13 row 38 歳出合計 equals the second for 3,063 of 3,063. The revenue leaves (rows 01-25 and 29) sum to their total exactly. The earlier 2.47x and 0.50x were measured against the importer's output, which caps detail at 360 rows per municipality, so they mixed an over-count from the hierarchy with an under-count from truncation and pointed at the wrong cause.

Japan's expenditure leaf natures sum to 歳出合計 for 2,825 of 3,063 municipalities; the other 238 exceed it by about 0.01%. Two reconciling candidates were tested and neither explains it — subtracting 歳入振替項目 (row 39) or 受託事業費 (row 26) changes nothing. The published figures are unaffected because they come from row 38 directly, and the discrepancy is recorded rather than absorbed into a tolerance wide enough to hide a real defect.

Two e-Stat file ids were needed and one of them cost an hour to a typo. 表5 収入の状況_2 is statInfId 000040375640; it was probed early and appeared to 404, because the id was assembled as a 7-digit prefix plus the 6-digit tail — thirteen digits rather than twelve. The portal's file listing is rendered client-side, so enumerating a year's files means driving it in a browser: toukei=00200251, tstat=000001077755, tclass1=000001077756, tclass2=000001077757, year=20250 lists all 124 CSVs for FY2024 with their table numbers. Note the year in that URL is the publication year, not the fiscal year — year=20240 returns FY2023 with unpadded entity codes.

Coverage was being judged by which countries had an entity directory rather than by what the warehouse holds, and that understated it badly. The warehouse carries 25 countries and 76,048 entities: France 35,042, Italy 7,896, Czechia 6,254, Spain 6,198, Brazil 5,557, Japan 2,982, Poland 2,486, Mexico 2,380, Peru 1,891, Ukraine 1,467 and the rest. France, Czechia, Poland, Ukraine, Britain and Sweden were never missing — they lacked directories, not facts, and they now have them. What is genuinely thin is the United States (4 entities loaded against 19,401 in the directory) and Germany (11 against 10,756), plus Norway, the Netherlands and Finland with none.

The eleven countries added from the international directory have identity but no headline rule, so they are not yet served from the warehouse. Deriving one needs a published baseline to check against, and for these countries that baseline is data/international-municipalities.v1.json rather than the fan-out the derivation currently reads. That is the next step for them: point the derivation at the second baseline, then the same gate admits them on the same evidence as the other fifteen.

Ukraine and Sweden have full warehouse coverage but cannot yet carry a headline, and the reason is scope rather than modelling. Summing each side at actual/FY gives Sweden revenue at a fifth of expenditure (378.6bn against 1,789.8bn for 2024, excluding summary rows) because se-scb-municipal-income covers external income and not kommunalskatt; and Ukraine at a half (1,185.6bn against 2,237.4bn) because ua-openbudget-incomes appears to exclude the inter-budget transfers that fund a large share of local spending. Authored rules were written for both, produced those ratios, and were withdrawn. Publishing them would show a Swedish municipality spending five times its income. Closing this needs the missing revenue series, not a different rule.

Poland generates cleanly from the warehouse but is not published, and the difference matters. Its 2,486 profiles have a median revenue-to-expenditure ratio of 1.001 across 4,956 entity-years, which is the shape of a budget that must balance — but they are written to .warehouse-profiles, which is gitignored and not in the image. The build ships the hydrated fan-out, and Poland has never been in it; there is one Polish page, the country index. Counting those profiles as published briefly credited the coverage contract with 2,486 profiles that ship nowhere, which is the overstatement that contract exists to prevent. The coverage builder now measures what ships and only reads warehouse profiles when WAREHOUSE_PROFILES_SHIP says they are part of it.

Nothing in the deployed image is built by scripts/build-profiles-from-warehouse.mjs. The generator, its verification against 54,502 published headlines, and the fifteen rebuilt countries are all real, but .warehouse-profiles is a local artifact: cloudbuild hydrates data/municipal-expansion from GCS and merges warehouse headlines and breakdowns into it via export-municipal-headlines and export-municipal-breakdowns. Making the generator the serving path means adding it as a build step with BigQuery access — which the build already has for those two exports — and publishing its output to the serving layer. Until then the generator proves the fan-out is reproducible; it does not replace it in production.

The deploy failed on verify-data-layers with 20 of 25 page groups showing matching file counts and mismatched hashes, and the cause was local drift rather than anything in GCS. Every international municipality page differed from the hosted copy by exactly six bytes — the cache-buster on municipal-expanded-profile.js, 20260828-fx-currency locally regenerated to 20260831-warehouse-lines-2 after that script was rewired to the warehouse endpoint — and the committed manifest had been built from the drifted local copies. The Czech pages differed more substantially and in the wrong direction: the local copies had lost the og:image tags the hosted ones carry. Local was re-synced from GCS and the manifest rebuilt from it, so the layer, the manifest and the deployed pages all describe the same bytes. Regenerating the pages against the current template is a real change worth making, and it is a reviewable one of its own rather than something to discover during a deploy.

The glossary is built and validated but reaches one term on one page. Marking a term wraps it in a span, which splits the text node it sits in, and budget-i18n.js matches whole text nodes against literal Czech keys — so marking a term inside a sentence that is itself a dictionary key silently stops that sentence translating. That happened on the first attempt, to a sentence about the general-government perimeter, and scripts/validate-glossary.mjs now fails the build on it. Surfacing the remaining 27 terms means either choosing positions whose text node is not a key, or moving the dictionary off literal-sentence keys — the second is the real fix and is a change of its own.

The licence audit is untouched and stays that way deliberately. All 81 declared sources lack verified terms — 31 recorded unverified, 50 unrecorded — and settling them means reading 81 publishers' conditions and deciding what redistribution each permits. A confident wrong answer there is worse than no answer, because the embed would then carry an explicit grant the source never gave. It needs a human read, or at minimum a per-publisher terms URL recorded without asserting what the terms allow.

France's published headline comes from OFGL, not from the DGFiP balances, and the hypothesis that it was an opérations d'ordre exclusion was wrong. Summing the balance accounts for FR:01001 gave revenue 995,320.87 and expenditure 2,366,440.01 against a published 914,157.60 and 2,285,276.74 — both sides differing by exactly 81,163.27, which is the signature of internal transfers and is not what this was. No subset of the commune's accounts summed to it because the published figures are not a balance sum: they are OFGL's own 'Recettes totales' and 'Dépenses totales', which match to the cent. Those six aggregates are now loaded for all 34,875 communes across both years — 418,260 rows, stored as summary rows because they are the publisher's totals of the balance facts beside them.

Two verification blind spots, both found by fixing them. The derivation attributed the international directory's single revenue and expenditure pair to every year an entity lists, so France scored 50% — a misread baseline reading as a half-broken rule; the pair belongs to the latest year. And the profile builder verified only against the fan-out, so a country that never had one — Czechia — reported 0 of 0 and looked like it had passed. With the directory as a second baseline it reports 12,508 of 12,508.

The deploy could not finish, and had not been able to for some time. hydrate-data-layers took 1,526 seconds of an 1,800-second build ceiling, leaving under five minutes for the exports, the 35,000-profile snapshot, the image build and the deploy; the next attempt was cancelled mid-hydration when the whole build hit the ceiling. The cost is per-file rather than per-byte — roughly 36,000 small objects across four layers, pulled one tree after another. They now hydrate concurrently with every exit status checked, and the ceiling is 3,600s. A layer failing silently would hydrate as empty and the verify step would blame the manifest, so a partial hydration is made to fail loudly instead.

France is built from the warehouse and reproduces every published headline: 69,750 of 69,750 across all 34,875 communes and both years. Getting there needed the fact query batched by entity — 7,244,504 rows will not return through the bq CLI in one buffer — and a second fix that only showed up at full scale. Ninety-seven communes report 2024 rather than 2025 and had no headline at all, because year stratification had been implemented once, on the fan-out baseline, and the international-directory baseline never got it. An even spread over 34,875 entities never sampled one of the 97, so no 2024 rule was derived and exactly those communes came out empty. Eighteen countries now build from the warehouse: sixteen derived and verified, two authored.

Britain has 552,003 facts across 374 authorities and still cannot carry a headline, for the same reason as Sweden and Ukraine: the revenue side is not revenue. It is grants — RG_granttot_tot_grant at 67.75bn for 2024 against RSX_totsx_tot_exp at 147.16bn of expenditure — and council tax and business rates, which fund the difference, are not in the dataset. Summing each side gives a median revenue-to-expenditure ratio of -0.038, negative because budget_side is unreliable here too: RSX_totsx_tot_inc, total income, is filed on the expenditure side. What is well defined and publishable is expenditure alone, either RSX_totsx_tot_exp or the net revenue expenditure MHCLG itself leads with, RS_netrevexp_net_exp at 57.85bn. The codes also nest — RS_sub_tot_net_exp and RS_netcurrtot_net_exp are totals containing one another — so any sum needs the summary rows resolved first.

Paraguay has 281,957 facts across 263 municipalities and no revenue side at all — every row is expenditure, 152 codes, 66,955bn PYG. There is nothing to derive a revenue headline from and nothing to authorise one against, so it stays unpublished until an income series is loaded.

Four countries now sit in the same category and it is worth naming as one rather than four: Sweden, Ukraine, Britain and Paraguay all have substantial fact coverage and an incomplete or mis-sided revenue series. In each case a headline could be produced and would be wrong — Sweden at a fifth of expenditure, Ukraine at a half, Britain negative, Paraguay absent. Each needs the missing income series, not a different rule, and publishing any of them would put a municipality on the site spending several times what it earns.

Vintages are now measurable for the municipal layer, which was not true when B4 was first recorded. Of 63 loaded source editions across 25 countries, 40 name a publisher edition in their source id — br-siconfi-rreo-2025, cz-monitor-finm-2025-12, pl-mf-rb27s-2024q4 — against 2 of 81 in the declared-source registry. The two sets overlap but are not the same: this one covers what is loaded, that one covers what artifacts declare. 23 loaded sources still name no edition, mostly the -municipal-expansion ids that predate the convention, and they are recorded without one rather than given the fiscal year their rows happen to cover. Those are different claims: de-aachen-budget-2026 is a 2026 publication covering 2026 to 2029.

B3's sovereign side is started. budget_detail.economic_observations was designed for exactly this — country, indicator, period, value, unit, observation status, and a source_vintage column — and had been sitting empty at zero rows. It now holds the IMF World Economic Outlook series behind sovereign-benchmark.v1.json: 52,583 observations across 191 countries and 15 metrics, 2005 to 2024, split 44,587 actual and 7,996 estimate. Round-tripping it against the artifact reproduces all 52,583 exactly, value and observation status together. The status matters as much as the value: charting an estimate as though it were an outturn is the commonest way a fiscal chart misleads, and the distinction was already in the data and not in the schema until now.

One artifact must not be generated from the warehouse, and it is worth saying why before someone tries. data/international-municipalities.v1.json is the published baseline the headline rules are derived and verified against — 105,416 entities with the revenue and expenditure the site shows. Regenerating it from the same warehouse those rules read would make every check circular: the generator would be proving it agrees with itself. It stays an independently maintained artifact for as long as it is the thing being checked against.

A serving layer that could replace the fan-out now exists and measures 17 files and 18.4 MB, against 28,559 files and 635 MB. It took two corrections to get there and both are worth keeping. First, the generated profiles were 1.4 GB across 72,174 files — larger than what they replace, because they carry complete warehouse detail where the fan-out was truncated. Dropping the detail array fixes that (1,108 MB to 18.4 MB) and is safe because the profile page prefers /public-data/municipality-lines and falls back to the file only when the endpoint has nothing. Second, slimming made the file count worse — 65,920 against 28,559 — and hydration cost is per-file, not per-byte: 36,000 objects took 1,526 seconds, 0.72 MB/s, nowhere near a network limit. So a slim fan-out would have hydrated slower while being thirty-five times smaller. One NDJSON per country removes both problems, and the serving snapshot it feeds is a single JSONL stream anyway.

The bundles now serve: prepare-public-serving-snapshots.mjs reads .warehouse-bundle/<cc>.ndjson where it exists and the directory where it does not, and they are hashed as the `bundles` layer. Czechia is deliberately excluded — it is not served by the lines endpoint, so a slim profile would have no detail and no way to fetch any, and the builder refuses it rather than shipping one; it is read from data/entities instead. France is read from its bundle but publishes nothing: its entities carry no url, so it has no canonical route, and it is query-driven through municipalities/france/profile/ instead.
